sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the construction, content and data quality of the reference data set RDS-NMD-NL-2025.1, which serves the Non-Maturity Deposit Model NL (NMD-NL) version 2.0, registered in the model inventory under model identifier MDL-12. The RDS covers the EUR non-maturity deposits of retail, SME and non-financial corporate customers of the Bank: current accounts and instant-access savings accounts without contractual maturity. NMD-NL estimates the stable and core parts of these deposits, the pass-through of market rates to client rates and the resulting replicating portfolio; its output is used in EVE and NII measurement, the supervisory outlier tests (SOT), the ICAAP, the hedging of the deposit portfolio and funds transfer pricing. The document follows the RDS template in Annex A of MRM-STD-021 v3.0, as required by ALM-STD-400 §10.4, and the data quality of the RDS has been assessed under MRM-STD-022 (chapter 6).

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS contains monthly observations from 31 January 2010 to 31 December 2024 (180 reference dates) of month-end balances, average balances, client rates, inflows and outflows for 34 product-segment cells, i.e. 6,120 cell-months, based on on average 4.6 million accounts per month (4.9 million at 31 December 2024); the target events are the monthly balance changes and client rate changes, of which 212 client rate changes across all products were observed. At 31 December 2024 the in-scope NMD balance was EUR 78.2 billion: retail transactional (R-TR) EUR 17.2 billion, retail non-transactional (R-NT) EUR 40.1 billion, SME transactional (SME-TR) EUR 9.3 billion, SME non-transactional (SME-NT) EUR 6.6 billion and non-financial wholesale operational deposits (NFW) EUR 5.0 billion. Deposits of financial customers (EUR 3.4 billion) are recorded in the RDS for reconciliation but are not behaviourally modelled (section 4.2).

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: With 15 years of monthly data the RDS exceeds the minimum of ten years required by ALM-STD-400 §5.6, and it includes two periods of rising interest rates (the ECB rate increases of April and July 2011 and the increase of the deposit facility rate from −0.50% to 4.00% between July 2022 and September 2023) as well as falling rates in 2011–2014 and from June 2024. It also includes the period of negative policy rates from June 2014 to July 2022, in which client rates on retail savings were floored at 0% and negative rates were charged only on balances above EUR 100,000 in 2021–2022, the inflow of pandemic savings in 2020–2021 and the migration of savings to term deposits in 2023. January 2010 is the first month after the migration of deposit administration to the current deposit system (DAS) with consistent product and segment codes, so the window uses the Bank's longest consistent own history.

sections.heading: Target variables and outcome horizon
sections.text: The model has two sets of target variables: for the volume model, the monthly log change of the month-end balance per product-segment cell, and for the pass-through model, the monthly change of the balance-weighted client rate per product. The outcome horizon of the volume model is the 10-year modelling horizon over which the stable part is derived; the pass-through model is estimated on monthly changes. Market rates are the ECB deposit facility rate, the euro short-term rate (€STR, with EONIA before October 2019) and the EUR swap curve; the ECB deposit facility rate is the primary driver of client rates in the Bank's pricing policy. Balances and rates are taken at product level because client rates are set per product and not per account.

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The RDS is sourced from the deposit administration system DAS (account balances, product codes, interest accruals), the customer master data of the CRM system (customer segment and ESA 2010 institutional sector), the Retail Pricing Database RPD (client rate history per product and rate tier), the liquidity reporting system LRS (LCR operational deposit flag), the general ledger (reconciliation) and the Market Data Hub (policy, €STR, Euribor and swap rates). For each type of data the authoritative source is defined in the Group Data Catalogue: DAS for balances, CRM for customer segment and sector, RPD for client rates, LRS for the operational deposit classification and the Market Data Hub for market rates. DAS records per account the product and interest rate code (the client rate is administered and reprices at the Bank's discretion), the withdrawal conditions (free withdrawal, notice or withdrawal fee on specific savings products) and the fee applicable on early withdrawal, and these fields are extracted into the RDS. Account-level data are aggregated in the Finance Data Warehouse (FDW) to product-segment cells before extraction; the RDS itself contains no account-level or customer-level data, and all in-scope NMD balances of the Bank's Dutch retail, SME and corporate business lines are captured.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Three exclusions are applied in the aggregation; shares are expressed as a percentage of the in-scope balance over the observation period. E1 – deposits of financial customers (ESA sector S.12, EUR 3.4 billion at 31 December 2024): excluded from modelling and treated as repricing overnight, in line with EBA/GL/2022/14 paragraph 110. E2 – balances of the online savings label acquired in 2014, for January 2010 to June 2015 before their migration to the Bank's products: 3.1% of R-NT balance-months, excluded because client rates were set by the former owner under a different pricing policy. E3 – blocked and pledged accounts and accounts in estate settlement: 0.9% of balance-months, excluded because withdrawal is not at the customer's discretion. For each exclusion the impact analysis in section 5.3 concludes that it does not materially affect the estimated stable parts or betas (largest effect: E2, +0.8 percentage points on the R-NT stable part).

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: The treatment of missing values is documented per variable in Annex C, distinguishing values missing at random, structurally missing values (for example rate tiers for products without tiering) and values missing because of a data deficiency. Missing client rates for 2010–2012 (DD-02) are reconstructed rather than imputed; the only imputation is the operational deposit share of NFW before 2015 (DD-03), which is set to the 2015 average share of 61% per product, and its effect on the NFW stable part is +1.2 percentage points compared with excluding the period. Outliers are identified by documented rules applied in development and production: monthly balance changes above five standard deviations of the cell and client rates outside −1% to 6%. The pandemic inflow months March–June 2020 are flagged as outliers and handled by a dummy in the volume model (EJ-NMD-04) rather than removed. No missing values occur in the target variables after reconstruction, and target values are not imputed.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: The RDS covers the full in-scope population at every reference date, so representativeness concerns changes in the composition and behaviour of the depositor base over time. The product mix and segment shares at 31 December 2024 are within the ranges observed in the RDS, but the digital channel share has increased strongly: 78% of R-NT balances are held by customers who use the mobile app, against 31% in 2012, which may increase the speed of outflows under stress compared with the history (limitation L-03). The RDS contains both periods with client rates at the floor and periods with active repricing, and the rising-rate period 2022–2023 provides 18 months of observations of upward pass-through, which is the basis for the asymmetric pass-through estimate. The RDS is therefore considered representative for the current portfolio, subject to limitation L-03.

sections.heading: DQ rules and thresholds
sections.text: For each of the 12 CDEs at least one DQ rule is defined per applicable mandatory dimension, 58 rules in total, and the reason is recorded where a dimension is not applicable (for example timeliness of the static product attributes). The rules are documented in Annex A and the 44 recurring rules are implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool (rule set DQM-ALM-NMD). Each rule has amber and red thresholds at least as strict as the defaults of MRM-STD-022 §4.3 (completeness amber below 98% and red below 95%, reconciliation differences amber above 0.5% and red above 1% of amount, logical consistency amber below 99% and red below 98%). For the target variables (month-end balance and client rate) stricter thresholds apply: reconciliation of balances to the general ledger amber above 0.1% and red above 0.25%, and completeness of client rates amber below 99.5% and red below 99%. No deviation from the default thresholds was requested.

sections.heading: DQ results and reconciliation

Consistency checks confirm that the sum of the cells equals the product totals and that balance changes equal inflows minus outflows plus interest for 99.8% of cell-months; the 2016 change in segment codes (DD-01) was assessed for consistency over the observation period. Timeliness: month-end balances are available in FDW on business day 2 and in the RDS extract on business day 3. The RDS is also reconciled with the deposit balances in the quarterly IRRBB supervisory reporting, with a maximum difference of 0.01% explained by accrued interest.

sections.heading: Data deficiencies
sections.text: The data deficiency log of NMD-NL contains four entries, each recording affected variables and segments, DQ dimension, cause, estimated impact, treatment, remediation owner and target date, and each cross-referenced to the limitations log in chapter 8 of the MDD. DD-01 (consistency): the CRM migration of 2016 reclassified 1.8% of balances between retail and SME; treated by back-casting the 2016 mapping table to 2010–2015 (evidenced correction); limitation L-05. DD-02 (completeness): client rates of four legacy savings products missing for 2010–2012 (6% of R-NT balance); reconstructed from rate announcements (EJ-NMD-06); closed. DD-03 (completeness): the LCR operational deposit flag is available only from 2015; NFW operational share imputed for 2010–2014; limitation L-06. DD-04 (accuracy): for 2021–2022 the recorded R-NT client rate is the headline rate and ignores negative rates on tiers above EUR 100,000; the effective rate is computed from tier data, available from 2020; closed. Each deficiency is treated by evidenced correction, reconstruction documented as expert judgement or imputation as a methodological adjustment, and the treatment is recorded in the log; DD-01 and DD-03 are registered in the Bank data issue register (DI-2025-0112 and DI-2025-0118) with impact, owner, remediation plan and target date. None of the deficiencies is rated high or critical, so no escalation to the Group Data Governance Committee or the Model Risk Committee is required.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the construction, content and data quality of the reference data set RDS-NMD-NL-2025.1, which serves the Non-Maturity Deposit Model NL (NMD-NL) version 2.0, registered in the model inventory under model identifier MDL-12. The RDS covers the EUR non-maturity deposits of retail, SME and non-financial corporate customers of the Bank: current accounts and instant-access savings accounts without contractual maturity. NMD-NL estimates the stable and core parts of these deposits, the pass-through of market rates to client rates and the resulting replicating portfolio; its output is used in EVE and NII measurement, the supervisory outlier tests (SOT), the ICAAP, the hedging of the deposit portfolio and funds transfer pricing. The document follows the RDS template in Annex A of MRM-STD-021 v3.0, as required by ALM-STD-400 §10.4, and the data quality of the RDS has been assessed under MRM-STD-022 (chapter 6).

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS contains monthly observations from 31 January 2010 to 31 December 2024 (180 reference dates) of month-end balances, average balances, client rates, inflows and outflows for 34 product-segment cells, i.e. 6,120 cell-months, based on on average 4.6 million accounts per month (4.9 million at 31 December 2024); the target events are the monthly balance changes and client rate changes, of which 212 client rate changes across all products were observed. At 31 December 2024 the in-scope NMD balance was EUR 78.2 billion: retail transactional (R-TR) EUR 17.2 billion, retail non-transactional (R-NT) EUR 40.1 billion, SME transactional (SME-TR) EUR 9.3 billion, SME non-transactional (SME-NT) EUR 6.6 billion and non-financial wholesale operational deposits (NFW) EUR 5.0 billion. Deposits of financial customers (EUR 3.4 billion) are recorded in the RDS for reconciliation but are not behaviourally modelled (section 4.2).

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: With 15 years of monthly data the RDS exceeds the minimum of ten years required by ALM-STD-400 §5.6, and it includes two periods of rising interest rates (the ECB rate increases of April and July 2011 and the increase of the deposit facility rate from −0.50% to 4.00% between July 2022 and September 2023) as well as falling rates in 2011–2014 and from June 2024. It also includes the period of negative policy rates from June 2014 to July 2022, in which client rates on retail savings were floored at 0% and negative rates were charged only on balances above EUR 100,000 in 2021–2022, the inflow of pandemic savings in 2020–2021 and the migration of savings to term deposits in 2023. January 2010 is the first month after the migration of deposit administration to the current deposit system (DAS) with consistent product and segment codes, so the window uses the Bank's longest consistent own history.

sections.heading: Target variables and outcome horizon
sections.text: The model has two sets of target variables: for the volume model, the monthly log change of the month-end balance per product-segment cell, and for the pass-through model, the monthly change of the balance-weighted client rate per product. The outcome horizon of the volume model is the 10-year modelling horizon over which the stable part is derived; the pass-through model is estimated on monthly changes. Market rates are the ECB deposit facility rate, the euro short-term rate (€STR, with EONIA before October 2019) and the EUR swap curve; the ECB deposit facility rate is the primary driver of client rates in the Bank's pricing policy. Balances and rates are taken at product level because client rates are set per product and not per account.

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The RDS is sourced from the deposit administration system DAS (account balances, product codes, interest accruals), the customer master data of the CRM system (customer segment and ESA 2010 institutional sector), the Retail Pricing Database RPD (client rate history per product and rate tier), the liquidity reporting system LRS (LCR operational deposit flag), the general ledger (reconciliation) and the Market Data Hub (policy, €STR, Euribor and swap rates). For each type of data the authoritative source is defined in the Group Data Catalogue: DAS for balances, CRM for customer segment and sector, RPD for client rates, LRS for the operational deposit classification and the Market Data Hub for market rates. DAS records per account the product and interest rate code (the client rate is administered and reprices at the Bank's discretion), the withdrawal conditions (free withdrawal, notice or withdrawal fee on specific savings products) and the fee applicable on early withdrawal, and these fields are extracted into the RDS. Account-level data are aggregated in the Finance Data Warehouse (FDW) to product-segment cells before extraction; the RDS itself contains no account-level or customer-level data, and all in-scope NMD balances of the Bank's Dutch retail, SME and corporate business lines are captured.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Three exclusions are applied in the aggregation; shares are expressed as a percentage of the in-scope balance over the observation period. E1 – deposits of financial customers (ESA sector S.12, EUR 3.4 billion at 31 December 2024): excluded from modelling and treated as repricing overnight, in line with EBA/GL/2022/14 paragraph 110. E2 – balances of the online savings label acquired in 2014, for January 2010 to June 2015 before their migration to the Bank's products: 3.1% of R-NT balance-months, excluded because client rates were set by the former owner under a different pricing policy. E3 – blocked and pledged accounts and accounts in estate settlement: 0.9% of balance-months, excluded because withdrawal is not at the customer's discretion. For each exclusion the impact analysis in section 5.3 concludes that it does not materially affect the estimated stable parts or betas (largest effect: E2, +0.8 percentage points on the R-NT stable part).

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: The treatment of missing values is documented per variable in Annex C, distinguishing values missing at random, structurally missing values (for example rate tiers for products without tiering) and values missing because of a data deficiency. Missing client rates for 2010–2012 (DD-02) are reconstructed rather than imputed; the only imputation is the operational deposit share of NFW before 2015 (DD-03), which is set to the 2015 average share of 61% per product, and its effect on the NFW stable part is +1.2 percentage points compared with excluding the period. Outliers are identified by documented rules applied in development and production: monthly balance changes above five standard deviations of the cell and client rates outside −1% to 6%. The pandemic inflow months March–June 2020 are flagged as outliers and handled by a dummy in the volume model (EJ-NMD-04) rather than removed. No missing values occur in the target variables after reconstruction, and target values are not imputed.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: The RDS covers the full in-scope population at every reference date, so representativeness concerns changes in the composition and behaviour of the depositor base over time. The product mix and segment shares at 31 December 2024 are within the ranges observed in the RDS, but the digital channel share has increased strongly: 78% of R-NT balances are held by customers who use the mobile app, against 31% in 2012, which may increase the speed of outflows under stress compared with the history (limitation L-03). The RDS contains both periods with client rates at the floor and periods with active repricing, and the rising-rate period 2022–2023 provides 18 months of observations of upward pass-through, which is the basis for the asymmetric pass-through estimate. The RDS is therefore considered representative for the current portfolio, subject to limitation L-03.

sections.heading: DQ rules and thresholds
sections.text: For each of the 12 CDEs at least one DQ rule is defined per applicable mandatory dimension, 58 rules in total, and the reason is recorded where a dimension is not applicable (for example timeliness of the static product attributes). The rules are documented in Annex A and the 44 recurring rules are implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool (rule set DQM-ALM-NMD). Each rule has amber and red thresholds at least as strict as the defaults of MRM-STD-022 §4.3 (completeness amber below 98% and red below 95%, reconciliation differences amber above 0.5% and red above 1% of amount, logical consistency amber below 99% and red below 98%). For the target variables (month-end balance and client rate) stricter thresholds apply: reconciliation of balances to the general ledger amber above 0.1% and red above 0.25%, and completeness of client rates amber below 99.5% and red below 99%. No deviation from the default thresholds was requested.

Consistency checks confirm that the sum of the cells equals the product totals and that balance changes equal inflows minus outflows plus interest for 99.8% of cell-months; the 2016 change in segment codes (DD-01) was assessed for consistency over the observation period. Timeliness: month-end balances are available in FDW on business day 2 and in the RDS extract on business day 3. The result of every rule per variable and dimension against its thresholds and the balance excluded per exclusion reason are reported in Annex C; no CDE breaches a red threshold. The RDS is also reconciled with the deposit balances in the quarterly IRRBB supervisory reporting, with a maximum difference of 0.01% explained by accrued interest.

sections.heading: Data deficiencies
sections.text: The data deficiency log of NMD-NL contains four entries, each recording affected variables and segments, DQ dimension, cause, estimated impact, treatment, remediation owner and target date, and each cross-referenced to the limitations log in chapter 8 of the MDD. DD-01 (consistency): the CRM migration of 2016 reclassified 1.8% of balances between retail and SME; treated by back-casting the 2016 mapping table to 2010–2015 (evidenced correction); limitation L-05. DD-02 (completeness): client rates of four legacy savings products missing for 2010–2012 (6% of R-NT balance); reconstructed from rate announcements (EJ-NMD-06); closed. DD-03 (completeness): the LCR operational deposit flag is available only from 2015; NFW operational share imputed for 2010–2014; limitation L-06. DD-04 (accuracy): for 2021–2022 the recorded R-NT client rate is the headline rate and ignores negative rates on tiers above EUR 100,000; the effective rate is computed from tier data, available from 2020; closed. Each deficiency is treated by evidenced correction, reconstruction documented as expert judgement or imputation as a methodological adjustment, and the treatment is recorded in the log; DD-01 and DD-03 are registered in the Bank data issue register (DI-2025-0112 and DI-2025-0118) with impact, owner, remediation plan and target date. None of the deficiencies is rated high or critical, so no escalation to the Group Data Governance Committee or the Model Risk Committee is required.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: NMD-NL v2.0 models the behavioural repricing of the Bank's non-maturity deposits; it is a model under MRM-POL-001 §3 because its quantitative output is used for risk measurement, hedging decisions and regulatory reporting, and it is managed across the full model lifecycle. The intended uses are the repricing profile of NMD in EVE and NII measurement, the supervisory outlier tests, the ICAAP internal capital for IRRBB and the hedging of the deposit portfolio by the Treasury ALM desk; the secondary use is funds transfer pricing of deposits. The range of application is the EUR current and instant-access savings accounts of retail, SME and non-financial corporate customers (EUR 78.2 billion at 31 December 2024); term deposits, notice deposits of financial customers and deposits of financial customers are outside the range of application. Version 2.0 replaces v1.4, which used symmetric betas estimated on 2010–2021 and a fixed replicating portfolio set in 2021. The IRRBB policy (ALM-POL-001 §6.3) specifies that current and savings accounts are treated behaviourally with the core part allocated over maturities up to ten years, and NMD-NL implements this treatment.

sections.heading: Model design
sections.text: NMD-NL consists of four components per segment: (A) a volume model that splits balances into a volatile and a stable part; (B) a rate-driven migration model for outflows to term deposits when market rates rise; (C) a pass-through model for client rates; and (D) a core/non-core split with a replicating portfolio that expresses the repricing profile of the core part. The model is conditional on the rate scenario: in every EVE, NII and SOT scenario the client rates follow the scenario path through the pass-through model and the volumes through the migration model, rather than being held constant. The output per segment is the repricing profile (tenor buckets from overnight to ten years) passed to the ALM engine, together with the scenario-dependent client rates for NII.

sections.heading: Segmentation
sections.text: The modelled portfolio is divided into five behaviourally homogeneous segments: retail transactional (R-TR, current accounts), retail non-transactional (R-NT, instant-access savings), SME transactional (SME-TR), SME non-transactional (SME-NT) and non-financial wholesale operational deposits (NFW). The segments differ in volatility (standard deviation of monthly log balance changes 1.1% for R-TR, 1.4% for R-NT, 2.6% for SME-TR, 3.3% for SME-NT and 6.9% for NFW) and in pricing (current accounts are unremunerated, savings rates follow market rates with a lag). Segment homogeneity was tested by comparing product-level pass-through estimates within each segment; products whose betas differ by more than 0.15 from the segment estimate are modelled with product-specific betas (two savings products with a fixed bonus rate).

sections.text: The EVE SOT is computed quarterly for the six scenarios parallel up, parallel down, steepener, flattener, short rates up and short rates down with the EUR shock sizes of Part A of the Annex to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/856 (parallel 200 bp, short 250 bp, long 100 bp). EUR represents 97.9% of non-trading book financial liabilities and 98.7% of assets, so the shocks are applied to EUR only, all other currencies being below the 5% threshold and EUR exceeding 90% coverage. The change in EVE is computed on a run-off balance sheet in which the core part runs off according to the replicating portfolio profile and the non-core part reprices overnight. Cash flows are discounted with the EUR €STR OIS curve without instrument-, sector- or entity-specific credit or liquidity spreads. For the EVE measures, commercial margins are excluded from the deposit cash flows, which are projected at the risk-free rate at inception given by the OIS rates of the replicating tranches, the same transparent methodology that is applied to all banking book instruments and business units and aligned with the hedging practice; the exclusion was notified to the ECB Joint Supervisory Team on 28 June 2024.

sections.heading: Use in NII measurement
sections.text: The NII SOT applies the parallel up and parallel down scenarios over a one-year horizon to all interest income and expenses regardless of maturity and accounting treatment. NII is computed on a constant balance sheet in which maturing replicating tranches and repricing balances are replaced with instruments of the same currency, amount and repricing period at recent margins (the average deposit margin of the last three months), and client rates follow the scenario through the pass-through model. NII measures include commercial margins, i.e. the difference between the replicating portfolio yield and the client rate. The NII outlier test flags a large decline where one-year NII falls by more than 5% of Tier 1 capital under either parallel scenario; with NMD-NL v2.0 the worst outcome at 31 December 2024 is −2.7% of Tier 1 capital (parallel down). The Bank uses both an NII+MV measure and an EVE measure, which together capture gap, basis and option risk; NMD-NL contributes the repricing gap of deposits and the option risk of the client rate floor.

sections.heading: Scenario application, rate floor and consistency of use
sections.text: Key behavioural assumptions are adjusted to each shock scenario: client rates follow the pass-through model with the 0% floor for retail and SME savings, and rate-driven migration reduces R-NT and SME-NT balances in the upward scenarios. The post-shock rate floor of −150 bp at immediate maturity, rising by 3 bp per year to 0% at 50 years, is applied to the EUR risk-free curve before client rates are derived, with lower observed rates used where applicable. The application of the model to the prescribed shock scenarios, including the rate floor, the post-shock pass-through and the migration of volumes, is demonstrated for all eight SOT scenarios in section 7.4 and in the parallel run of the implementation report. sections.heading: Methodology
sections.text: Three alternatives were assessed for the volume model (a static historical-minimum approach, a quantile regression on balance changes and a simulated time-series model) and three for pass-through (a static beta, an error-correction model and an autoregressive distributed-lag model), against documented criteria: regulatory requirements of ALM-STD-400 §5, data availability, out-of-time accuracy, stability, interpretability and implementability. The simulated time-series volume model was selected because it provides a stable part at a defined confidence level over the modelling horizon, and the error-correction pass-through model because it separates the long-term beta from the speed of adjustment and allows asymmetry and the floor; the autoregressive distributed-lag model fitted slightly better in sample (tracking error 5 bp against 6 bp) but produced implausible sign changes of lag coefficients and was retained only as a benchmark.

sections.heading: Volume model and stable part
sections.text: For each segment the log balance is modelled as a linear trend with monthly seasonality and AR(1) residuals, and the stable part is the balance that remains with a confidence level of 99% over the 10-year modelling horizon, derived from the 1st percentile of 10,000 simulated balance paths with the trend growth capped at zero. The resulting stable parts at 31 December 2024 are R-TR 81%, R-NT 72%, SME-TR 63%, SME-NT 54% and NFW 41% of the balance; the volatile part is treated as repricing overnight. The stable part is recalculated monthly in production from the current balance, and its parameters (trend, seasonality, residual volatility) are re-estimated annually.

The stable-part assumptions for the retail segments are at least as conservative as the 12-month cumulative outflows of the internal liquidity stress test (R-TR stable part 81% against a maximum of 86%, R-NT 72% against a maximum of 76%); for the SME and NFW segments the comparison will be performed after the 2025 recalibration of the liquidity stress test. sections.heading: Pass-through model
sections.text: Client rates per product are modelled with an error-correction model on the ECB deposit facility rate, estimating the long-term beta and the speed of adjustment separately for rising and falling rates, with the 0% floor on retail and SME client rates imposed through a censored specification, over the period 2010–2023 that includes falling rates, rates at the floor and the rising-rate period 2022–2023. sections.heading: Core part and replicating portfolio
sections.text: The core part, i.e. the deposits that are stable and unlikely to reprice even under significant changes in market rates, is derived per segment as the stable part multiplied by one minus the higher of the rising and falling long-term betas: R-TR 81.0%, R-NT 38.2%, SME-TR 59.9%, SME-NT 21.6% and NFW 8.2% of the balance. The repricing profile of the core part is expressed through a replicating portfolio of rolling tranches (1 month to 10 years), whose weights are set by minimising the tracking error between the yield of the tranche portfolio and the client rate response implied by the estimated pass-through model over 2010–2023; margin stability is reported only as a diagnostic and is not part of the objective. sections.heading: Driver selection and economic rationale
sections.text: Candidate drivers were assessed for economic rationale, availability at the monthly production run and stability over time: the deposit facility rate, €STR, 3-month Euribor, the one-year term deposit rate, the savings rates of the three largest Dutch competitors and the household disposable income growth; competitor rates were rejected because they are not available at the point of use in a controlled form. Selection used univariate fit, likelihood-ratio tests of nested specifications and a correlation analysis in which, of correlated market rates (correlation above 0.95 for the deposit facility rate, €STR and Euribor), the deposit facility rate was retained because it drives the Bank's pricing policy; all final coefficients have signs consistent with economic intuition (positive betas below one, negative error-correction coefficients, positive migration sensitivity to the term deposit spread).

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: NMD-NL v2.0 models the behavioural repricing of the Bank's non-maturity deposits; it is a model under MRM-POL-001 §3 because its quantitative output is used for risk measurement, hedging decisions and regulatory reporting, and it is managed across the full model lifecycle. The intended uses are the repricing profile of NMD in EVE and NII measurement, the supervisory outlier tests, the ICAAP internal capital for IRRBB and the hedging of the deposit portfolio by the Treasury ALM desk; the secondary use is funds transfer pricing of deposits. The range of application is the EUR current and instant-access savings accounts of retail, SME and non-financial corporate customers (EUR 78.2 billion at 31 December 2024); term deposits, notice deposits of financial customers and deposits of financial customers are outside the range of application. Version 2.0 replaces v1.4, which used symmetric betas estimated on 2010–2021 and a fixed replicating portfolio set in 2021. The IRRBB policy (ALM-POL-001 §6.3) specifies that current and savings accounts are treated behaviourally with the core part allocated over maturities up to ten years, and NMD-NL implements this treatment.

sections.text: NMD-NL consists of four components per segment: (A) a volume model that splits balances into a volatile and a stable part; (B) a rate-driven migration model for outflows to term deposits when market rates rise; (C) a pass-through model for client rates; and (D) a core/non-core split with a replicating portfolio that expresses the repricing profile of the core part. The model is conditional on the rate scenario: in every EVE, NII and SOT scenario the client rates follow the scenario path through the pass-through model and the volumes through the migration model, rather than being held constant. The output per segment is the repricing profile (tenor buckets from overnight to ten years) passed to the ALM engine, together with the scenario-dependent client rates for NII.

sections.heading: Segmentation
sections.text: The modelled portfolio is divided into five behaviourally homogeneous segments: retail transactional (R-TR, current accounts), retail non-transactional (R-NT, instant-access savings), SME transactional (SME-TR), SME non-transactional (SME-NT) and non-financial wholesale operational deposits (NFW). The segments differ in volatility (standard deviation of monthly log balance changes 1.1% for R-TR, 1.4% for R-NT, 2.6% for SME-TR, 3.3% for SME-NT and 6.9% for NFW) and in pricing (current accounts are unremunerated, savings rates follow market rates with a lag). Segment homogeneity was tested by comparing product-level pass-through estimates within each segment; products whose betas differ by more than 0.15 from the segment estimate are modelled with product-specific betas (two savings products with a fixed bonus rate).

sections.heading: Financial customers and the regulatory cap
sections.text: Non-maturity deposits of financial customers (EUR 3.4 billion) are not behaviourally modelled and are treated as repricing overnight; this includes the operational part of EUR 0.3 billion, for which the Bank does not use the exception for operational deposits under Article 27(1)(a) of the LCR Delegated Regulation. Term deposits are modelled separately with the early redemption assumptions of ALM-STD-400 §6.5 and are outside the scope of this model.

sections.heading: Use in EVE measurement and the supervisory outlier test
sections.text: The EVE SOT is computed quarterly for the six scenarios parallel up, parallel down, steepener, flattener, short rates up and short rates down with the EUR shock sizes of Part A of the Annex to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/856 (parallel 200 bp, short 250 bp, long 100 bp). EUR represents 97.9% of non-trading book financial liabilities and 98.7% of assets, so the shocks are applied to EUR only, all other currencies being below the 5% threshold and EUR exceeding 90% coverage. The change in EVE is computed on a run-off balance sheet in which the core part runs off according to the replicating portfolio profile and the non-core part reprices overnight. Cash flows are discounted with the EUR €STR OIS curve without instrument-, sector- or entity-specific credit or liquidity spreads. sections.heading: Use in NII measurement
sections.text: The NII SOT applies the parallel up and parallel down scenarios over a one-year horizon to all interest income and expenses regardless of maturity and accounting treatment. NII is computed on a constant balance sheet in which maturing replicating tranches and repricing balances are replaced with instruments of the same currency, amount and repricing period at recent margins (the average deposit margin of the last three months), and client rates follow the scenario through the pass-through model. NII measures include commercial margins, i.e. the difference between the replicating portfolio yield and the client rate. The NII outlier test flags a large decline where one-year NII falls by more than 5% of Tier 1 capital under either parallel scenario; with NMD-NL v2.0 the worst outcome at 31 December 2024 is −2.7% of Tier 1 capital (parallel down). The Bank uses both an NII+MV measure and an EVE measure, which together capture gap, basis and option risk; NMD-NL contributes the repricing gap of deposits and the option risk of the client rate floor.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: The model is estimated on the frozen reference data set RDS-NMD-NL-2025.1 (monthly data January 2010 – December 2024, 34 product-segment cells), documented in EVD-12-RDS version 1.0 approved on 28 February 2025. The imputation of the NFW operational share before 2015 (DD-03) increases the NFW stable part by 1.2 percentage points compared with excluding the period, which is recorded in limitation L-06. The pandemic inflow months of 2020 are treated as outliers through a dummy in the volume model, applied consistently in the production re-estimation, and removing the dummy would reduce the R-NT stable part by 0.9 percentage points.

sections.heading: Estimation and out-of-time samples
sections.text: Before estimation, the development window was set to January 2010 – December 2023 and the out-of-time sample to January – December 2024, which contains the first rate cuts of the current cycle; because the data are aggregated time series, no random out-of-sample split is possible, and stability is instead tested by rolling-window estimation. The out-of-time year was not used for variable selection or parameter estimation, and the parameters reported in chapter 5 are those estimated on 2010–2023. The development window contains 168 months, of which 18 months in the rising-rate period July 2022 – December 2023.

sections.heading: Methodology
sections.text: Three alternatives were assessed for the volume model (a static historical-minimum approach, a quantile regression on balance changes and a simulated time-series model) and three for pass-through (a static beta, an error-correction model and an autoregressive distributed-lag model), against documented criteria: regulatory requirements of ALM-STD-400 §5, data availability, out-of-time accuracy, stability, interpretability and implementability. The simulated time-series volume model was selected because it provides a stable part at a defined confidence level over the modelling horizon, and the error-correction pass-through model because it separates the long-term beta from the speed of adjustment and allows asymmetry and the floor; the autoregressive distributed-lag model fitted slightly better in sample (tracking error 5 bp against 6 bp) but produced implausible sign changes of lag coefficients and was retained only as a benchmark.

sections.heading: Volume model and stable part
sections.text: For each segment the log balance is modelled as a linear trend with monthly seasonality and AR(1) residuals, and the stable part is the balance that remains with a confidence level of 99% over the 10-year modelling horizon, derived from the 1st percentile of 10,000 simulated balance paths with the trend growth capped at zero. The resulting stable parts at 31 December 2024 are R-TR 81%, R-NT 72%, SME-TR 63%, SME-NT 54% and NFW 41% of the balance; the volatile part is treated as repricing overnight. The stable part is recalculated monthly in production from the current balance, and its parameters (trend, seasonality, residual volatility) are re-estimated annually.

sections.heading: Rate-driven migration and volume stress
sections.text: Stability of volumes under stress is assessed with a rate-driven migration model, estimated on 2022–2024, in which 2.1% of the R-NT balance and 3.4% of the SME-NT balance migrate to term deposits per 100 bp of positive spread between the one-year term deposit rate and the savings rate within 12 months, and with a digital outflow scenario of 12% of R-NT and 15% of SME-NT balances within ten days (EJ-NMD-03). The stable-part assumptions for the retail segments are at least as conservative as the 12-month cumulative outflows of the internal liquidity stress test (R-TR stable part 81% against a maximum of 86%, R-NT 72% against a maximum of 76%); for the SME and NFW segments the comparison will be performed after the 2025 recalibration of the liquidity stress test. In the 2023 migration to term deposits, R-NT balances fell by EUR 3.3 billion (8.1%), which remained above the modelled stable part in every month.

sections.heading: Core part and replicating portfolio
sections.text: The core part, i.e. the deposits that are stable and unlikely to reprice even under significant changes in market rates, is derived per segment as the stable part multiplied by one minus the higher of the rising and falling long-term betas: R-TR 81.0%, R-NT 38.2%, SME-TR 59.9%, SME-NT 21.6% and NFW 8.2% of the balance. sections.heading: Driver selection and economic rationale
sections.text: Candidate drivers were assessed for economic rationale, availability at the monthly production run and stability over time: the deposit facility rate, €STR, 3-month Euribor, the one-year term deposit rate, the savings rates of the three largest Dutch competitors and the household disposable income growth; competitor rates were rejected because they are not available at the point of use in a controlled form. Selection used univariate fit, likelihood-ratio tests of nested specifications and a correlation analysis in which, of correlated market rates (correlation above 0.95 for the deposit facility rate, €STR and Euribor), the deposit facility rate was retained because it drives the Bank's pricing policy; all final coefficients have signs consistent with economic intuition (positive betas below one, negative error-correction coefficients, positive migration sensitivity to the term deposit spread).

sections.heading: Stress testing of behavioural assumptions
sections.text: For the Bank's stress-testing framework, NMD-NL provides stress variants with changes in depositor behaviour (the digital outflow scenario, a doubled migration to term deposits and betas of 0.60 for all savings segments), which are included in the ICAAP adverse scenario and in the Bank's reverse stress test on liquidity and earnings. The variants include a breakdown of the key assumptions of stability and pass-through, in which the stable part of R-NT falls to 55% and pass-through becomes symmetric at the higher beta. The largest EVE effect is the stable-part breakdown in the parallel up scenario (−EUR 241 million).

sections.heading: Assumptions and limitations
sections.text: The material assumptions have been identified and assessed for plausibility: (a) depositor behaviour in 2010–2023 is representative of future behaviour, including under rising rates; (b) the Bank's pricing policy continues to link savings rates to the deposit facility rate; (c) no growth is credited to the stable part; (d) client rates on retail and SME savings are floored at 0%; (e) the model is used at segment level and not for individual customers. The key behavioural assumptions are documented in this MDD, justified by the Bank's own history, aligned with the Treasury funding strategy and the deposit pricing policy, and tested annually; the materiality thresholds of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/857 are applied proportionately in deciding which assumptions are scenario-dependent. All inputs, assumptions and specification choices are documented and explained in chapters 3, 4 and 8 so that they are included in the independent validation. No third-party behavioural inputs are used; the vendor ALM engine only applies the repricing profiles and client rates produced by NMD-NL.

sections.heading: Individual expert judgements
sections.text: EJ-NMD-01 (design, high): the trend growth of balances is capped at zero in the stable-part simulation, because deposit growth after 2014 was driven by low rates and pandemic savings and cannot be relied upon for a 10-year horizon; the rejected alternative was the estimated trend of +3.1% per year for R-NT; impact −0.19 years on the combined average repricing maturity (−12%) and −EUR 96 million EVE parallel up. EJ-NMD-03 (design, medium): digital outflow stress severity of 12% (R-NT) and 15% (SME-NT) in ten days, based on published outflows of failed banks in 2023 scaled to the Bank's deposit guarantee coverage; impact assessed qualitatively. EJ-NMD-04 (design, low): pandemic dummy for March–June 2020. EJ-NMD-05 (calibration, medium): SME-TR beta set to 0.05 in line with the pricing policy because the estimate (0.03, standard error 0.04) is not significant. EJ-NMD-06 (data, low): reconstruction of legacy client rates.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This report presents the 2026 annual back-testing, sensitivity analysis and model review of NMD-NL v2.0 (model MDL-12) under ALM-STD-400 §8 and MRM-STD-040 §9. The NFW deviation is again driven by a small number of large corporate clients and is within the range expected under limitation L-04. The R-NT balance grew by 3.0% in 2026, mainly from interest capitalisation and inflows to the Bank's new savings product.

deficiencies.rationale: Stress assessment of volumes covers digital outflows and rate-driven migration, but the stable part is shown to be at least as conservative as the liquidity stress test only for the retail segments; the comparison for SME-NT and NFW has been postponed twice (MDD §4.2, BTR §4).

mitigation.text: Complete the comparison of the SME-TR, SME-NT and NFW stable parts with the internal liquidity stress test outflows and adjust the stable parts where they are less conservative.

deficiencies.rationale: The amber NFW balance forecast error (K1, −6.8%) is reported as 'under analysis'; the monitoring report does not document its cause, although the segment has been amber in three of the last four quarters.

mitigation.text: Document the cause of the NFW amber result (client concentration) and assess whether the NFW stable part or segment definition needs to change.

deficiencies.rationale: The impact of EJ-NMD-03 (digital outflow stress severity) is assessed only qualitatively, yet the judgement is classified as medium; for a Tier 1 model an unquantified judgement must be classified as high and approved by the MRC.

mitigation.text: Quantify the effect of EJ-NMD-03 on the stable parts and EVE, or reclassify it as high materiality and submit it to the MRC after Model Validation review.

deficiencies.rationale: The pass-through model is documented with asymmetric betas estimated over rising and falling periods, but the validator's sub-period estimation on July 2022 – December 2024 gives an R-NT rising-rate beta of 0.58 against the model's 0.42; the full-sample estimate is dominated by the long floor period and understates pass-through in a rising-rate environment.

mitigation.text: Re-estimate the rising-rate beta with a regime-dependent specification (floor versus non-floor periods) and quantify the NII and EVE impact of a beta of 0.58 for R-NT.

deficiencies.rationale: The 2026 client-rate back-test is performed with pass-through parameters re-estimated on data including 2026, so it is an in-sample fit rather than a test of the production parameters; with the production parameters the R-NT tracking error is 14 bp (amber), not 8 bp (green).

mitigation.text: Back-test with the parameters in production during the back-testing period and report re-estimated parameters only as beta-drift information.
